newsitem.title: USA: Ozone group leaves new utility controls up to EPA.
newsitem.headline: Ozone group leaves new utility controls up to EPA.

text.p: Eastern U.S. states agreed to ask the Environmental Protection Agency to require power plants to cut their emissions by as much as 85 percent, industry and environmental officials said Monday.

At a final meeting set for June 19, capping a two-year project to determine how much pollution blows from one area to another, the states are set to recommend that utilities should have to cut emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) by 50 to 85 percent from projected levels for 2007.

EPA created the Ozone Transport Assessment Group of 37 eastern states in 1995 to tackle the problem of NOx emissions as it grew clear that major urban areas would be unable to meet existing clean air standards.

At its final meeting next week, the group is set to discuss strategies to control pollution from sources such as cars and manufacturing plants, but utility emissions, addressed last week, are expected to be the biggest target.

"(The group) basically recommended stringent region-wide emissions cuts from utilities are the most effective and economically efficient way to address the ozone problem," said Jason Grumet, executive director of Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management.

States where pollution is within U.S. standards but which are contributing to air quality problems downwind said they should not have to curb utility emissions more than already required under the Clean Air Act acid rain program -- which calls for about a 50 percent cut NOx emissions.
Downwind states, largely in the Northeast, which are struggling to meet federal clean air standards, called for more sweeping cuts.
The group is now putting the ball back into EPA's hands to use research done over the last two years to set emissions "budgets" for about 33 states.

"EPA's driving the ship now," said Patrick DalPorto, staff engineer for environmental strategies at American Electric Power, one of the companies battling strict new limits which could be imposed on coal-fired power plants.

Merrylin Zaw-Mon, director of air and radiation for Maryland's Environment Department, predicted that in most areas utilities would be forced to cut their emissions beyond existing regulations in order to help stem the flow of smog into badly polluted areas.

Utilities say the final outcome is unfair, arguing that research so far shows that even with big emissions cuts in areas like the Midwest, air quality in the Northeast would still not be up to standard.

"You get the greatest benefit in the area closest to the (emissions) reductions," said AEP's DalPorto, adding that it would be up to state agencies to decide how to meet the emissions limits that EPA will set for each state.
